summary: This unit covers hand soldering and de-soldering of electrical and electronic parts at Level 3: planning a repair, isolating equipment, controlling static, choosing solder, flux, tips and temperatures, and making sound joints on boards, wires and terminals. You will learn to control heat on difficult boards, remove and replace through-hole and surface-mount parts without damage, inspect work against a written standard, test a repaired board safely, keep records and supervise others at the bench.

blocks.p: Soldering joins metal parts with a filler metal, **solder**, that melts at a much lower temperature than the parts themselves. An electrician meets it in control boards for pumps, gates, alarms, air-conditioners and generators, in LED drivers, and in low-voltage control wiring and connectors. **De-soldering** is taking a joint apart again without harming the board or the part.

This unit is for Level 3 trainees. Making one neat joint on a practice board is Level 2 work. At Level 3 you plan and carry out a repair on someone's equipment: you find out how the board was made, protect it from static and heat, choose the method for each joint, inspect against a written standard, test before the board goes back, record what you did, and guide others at the bench.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the work
Find out the solder type, the maker's rework rules and the parts needed; estimate the time; prepare the bench.
Make the equipment safe
Isolate, lock off and prove the equipment dead, and check that capacitors have discharged, before a board is removed.
Work safely at the bench
Control fumes, lead, burns, splashes and fire risks, and deal with waste properly.
Control static (ESD)
Set up and check an ESD-protected bench, and handle sensitive parts correctly.
Choose and look after equipment
Choose the iron, tip, temperature, solder and flux for each joint; keep tips and tools in good order.
Solder through-hole parts, wires and terminals
Make well-wetted joints with the right amount of solder, and know when a crimp or screw connection is the better choice.
Control heat
Deal with heavy copper, multilayer boards and heat-sensitive parts without cold joints or board damage.
De-solder and rework
Remove and replace through-hole and surface-mount parts, clear bridges and repair damaged tracks by approved methods.
Inspect, test and record
Inspect against the workmanship standard, test without power and then with a limited supply, and complete the rework record.
Supervise others
Set and check bench rules, and correct poor technique by showing the right way.

ul: Equipment comes from many countries. Newer boards are nearly all **lead-free**; older equipment and some repair benches still use **tin-lead** solder. You must find out which you are dealing with.
Mains supplies are **110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz**. A board from a mains panel is removed only after safe isolation.
Humid, salty air helps to limit static, but it corrodes boards and joints; air-conditioned workshops are dry, and static builds up easily there.
Replacement boards can take weeks to arrive from overseas, which is why careful board-level repair is valuable, and why a board damaged by a careless repair is expensive.

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, then try the practice test and read every explanation. Temperatures and times in these notes are typical figures: always follow the maker of the solder, the station and the equipment, and your instructor.

sections.title: Planning the work and making the equipment safe

blocks.h: Find out before you heat anything

head: Find out
Where
Why
rows: Which solder the board was made with
A 'Pb-free' or 'RoHS' mark on the board, the service manual, the maker
Lead-free and tin-lead need different temperatures and should not be mixed on one joint
The maker's rework rules
The service manual or the customer's instructions
Limits on temperature, number of reworks, cleaning, and coatings that must be removed and replaced
The exact part and its orientation
The parts list, the circuit reference printed on the board (R12, C4, U3), a photo taken before removal
A wrong or reversed part can destroy the board at power-up
Whether the board is static-sensitive
The ESD symbol on the board or its bag; assume yes for any board with ICs
Sets the handling rules
Whether the board has a protective (conformal) coating
Look for a clear glossy film
It must be removed locally before soldering and replaced afterwards, as the maker says
How the repair will be tested
The service manual, test points, the customer
You plan the test before you start, not after

blocks.p: Count the joints and allow a time for each, then add time for setting up, inspection, cleaning, testing and the record. If a board has 30 joints to rework at about 40 seconds each, the soldering itself is 30 × 40 = 1,200 seconds = **20 minutes**; the whole job may be an hour or more.

blocks.h: Taking a board out of mains equipment

flow: Tell the user and agree the shutdown
Isolate the equipment at its breaker or isolator, not just its front switch
Lock off and tag
Prove dead with a two-pole tester checked on a proving unit before and after
Check that large capacitors have discharged; discharge them safely if not
Label or photograph every connector and cable
Take anti-static precautions, remove the board and put it in an anti-static bag

blocks.p: Large capacitors in power supplies, motor drives, inverters and UPS units can hold a **dangerous charge for minutes or hours after the power is off**. The mains filter capacitor on a 220 V supply can sit at about 300 V DC. Before touching the board, measure the voltage across the capacitor with a suitable meter. If it has not fallen to a safe level, discharge it through a suitable resistor or a discharge tool, as the maker says, and measure again. Never short a capacitor with a screwdriver: the bang can damage the capacitor, the board and your eyes.

blocks.note: The front on/off switch of a panel or appliance often switches only the control circuit. The supply terminals, the transformer and parts of the board stay live. Isolate at the supply, lock off and prove dead.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Health and safety at the bench

head: Hazard
What can happen
Control
rows: Flux fumes
Rosin (colophony) fumes irritate the eyes and lungs and can cause asthma that lasts for life
A fume extractor with its intake **close to the joint**, drawing the fumes away from your face; clean or change its filter as the maker says; do not lean over the work
Lead (in tin-lead solder)
Lead gets into the body from the hands to the mouth, and builds up
No eating, drinking or smoking at the bench; wash hands before breaks and at the end of the session; keep food and cups away
Burns
The tip is at 300 °C or more; fresh joints and parts stay hot
Iron always back in its stand; never reach across it; let work cool; know where the cold water is
Splashes of molten solder
Solder in the eye or on the skin
Safety glasses; never flick or shake solder off the tip, wipe it off on the cleaner; cut leads so they cannot fly
Fire
A hot iron on paper, solvent or a plastic bench
A proper stand; flammable cleaners capped and away from the iron; iron off when you leave the bench
Solvents (isopropyl alcohol, flux cleaner)
Flammable; vapour and skin contact
Small amounts, good ventilation, away from heat; gloves if the label says so
Hot air tools and heat guns
Burns; scorching things behind the work
Point away from people and cables; let the nozzle cool on its stand
Electric shock
A damaged station lead; a board that is still charged or connected
Check the station's lead and plug; work only on isolated, discharged boards

blocks.p: Solder waste, used braid, tip-cleaning waste and **dross** (the oxide skin skimmed off a solder pot) contain metals that must not go in ordinary rubbish. Collect them in a marked, lidded container and dispose of them by the Centre's or company's procedure. Used solvent wipes go in a closed metal bin.

blocks.h: Bench rules a team leader sets

ul: Extraction on and placed before the first joint.
Safety glasses on for soldering and for cutting leads.
Irons in stands; no flicking solder; no unattended hot irons.
No food or drink; hands washed before breaks.
Boards isolated and capacitors discharged before work.
Wrist straps tested and recorded before sensitive parts are handled.
Waste in the marked container.

blocks.p: Explain the reason for each rule at a short briefing, post the rules at the bench, and check them by walking round during the session: look at the extractor, the strap test record and the stands. Correct people straight away, and record and report problems that keep coming back.

blocks.note: For a burn, cool the skin under cool running water for about 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter or toothpaste. Report every burn and every splash to the eye.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Electrostatic discharge (ESD)** is the sudden flow of static charge from one object to another. You feel a spark only above about 3,000 V, but many ICs and transistors are damaged by less than 100 V. The damage may kill a part at once, or weaken it so that it fails weeks later in the customer's equipment. You cannot see either kind, so you prevent both.
An **EPA** is a marked area where everything that could hold a charge is either connected to earth in a controlled way or kept out.

head: Item
What it does
Points to check
rows: Wrist strap and lead
Drains charge from your body to earth
Snug on bare skin; lead clipped to the bench's earth point. The lead contains a resistor of about **1 MΩ** (1,000,000 Ω), which limits the current through you if you touch a live part while strapped.
Dissipative bench mat
Lets charge on tools, boards and parts drain away slowly
Its earth lead must be connected to the common earth point. A mat that is not connected does nothing.
Common earth point
Brings the strap, the mat and the equipment to the same potential
Connected to the installation's protective earth as the maker of the kit says
Earthed (ESD-safe) soldering station
Keeps the tip at earth potential
Check the station's lead and its tip-to-earth connection at set times
Heel straps or ESD footwear, with a suitable floor
Earth people who move about
They work only on a conductive or dissipative floor
Anti-static bags, tubes and trays
Protect parts and boards outside the EPA
Shielding (silvery) bags protect from outside charge; pink bags only avoid making charge

blocks.p: Ordinary plastics and synthetic materials hold a charge and cannot be earthed: plastic bags, bubble wrap, styrofoam cups and packing, sticky tape, plastic document sleeves, synthetic clothing brushing the work. Keep them off an ESD bench. Paper and cardboard are best kept away too.

ul: Test each **wrist strap on a strap tester** before each session of work, while wearing it, and record the result. A strap can fail without any sign: a broken wire inside the lead, a worn band, dry skin.
A person whose strap fails does not handle sensitive parts until the strap is replaced and passes.
Check the mat's earth lead and the earth point at set times with a suitable meter, and record it.
Keep the mat clean with the maker's cleaner: ordinary polish leaves an insulating film.
Keep parts and boards in their protective packaging until they are at the bench and you are strapped.
Hold boards by their edges; do not touch pins, pads or connector contacts.
Put a board down only on the mat, never on a chair, a plastic tray or a pile of paper.
Use the bag for transport even inside the workshop.

blocks.note: Dry air lets static build up much more easily than humid air. An air-conditioned Jamaican workshop can be as dry as anywhere in the world, so do not rely on the climate: use the strap and the mat every time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A temperature-controlled station holds the tip at the temperature you set and brings it back quickly after each joint. Choose the **tip** before you touch the temperature dial: the tip's size and shape decide how fast heat flows into the joint.

head: Tip
Use
rows: Chisel (screwdriver) tip
The general choice: its flat face gives good contact. Pick a width about the same as the pad.
Large chisel
Heavy leads, large pads, earth planes, wire to terminals
Fine conical tip
Very small pads and tight spaces only; it carries little heat
Bevel (hoof) or knife tip
Drag soldering rows of surface-mount pins; clearing bridges

head: Solder
Melts at about
Typical tip setting
rows: 63/37 tin-lead
About 300 to 350 °C
60/40 tin-lead
183 to about 190 °C
About 300 to 350 °C
Lead-free tin-silver-copper (SAC)
About 340 to 380 °C

blocks.p: Use the **lowest setting that makes a good joint in about 2 to 4 seconds**. A setting that is much too high burns the flux before it has done its work, oxidises the tip, lifts pads and damages parts. If a joint will not flow, the cure is usually a bigger tip, a cleaner tip or fresh flux, not more degrees. Follow the solder maker's and the equipment maker's figures.

Check the **real tip temperature** with a **tip thermometer** (a small instrument with a sensor pad that you tin and touch with the tip), at set times and whenever joints start to behave oddly. A station's display shows what it is aiming for, not always what the tip has reached.

head: Alloy
Points
rows: 63/37 tin-lead
**Eutectic**: it goes straight from liquid to solid at 183 °C, with no pasty stage, so a joint is less likely to be spoiled by movement as it sets. Flows easily. Contains lead.
60/40 tin-lead
Has a short pasty range while it sets; a joint moved during that time becomes dull and weak. Contains lead.
Lead-free SAC (tin, silver, copper)
Melts about 34 °C higher than 63/37, wets more slowly and needs more heat; wears tips faster. A good joint looks a little duller and grainier than tin-lead.

blocks.p: **Do not mix** lead-free and tin-lead solder on one joint unless the maker allows it. The mixture can form a weaker joint that cracks in service. Use the alloy the board was made with, keep separate tips, braid and solder reels for each, and label them.

Hot metal oxidises in seconds, and solder will not bond to oxide. **Flux** removes the oxide, protects the hot surfaces and helps the solder to flow. Solder wire has flux in its core; it is released as the wire melts **on the joint**.

head: Type
Residue
After soldering
rows: Rosin (or resin) flux
Sticky amber residue, mostly harmless when cold
Clean off if the standard or the customer asks, usually with isopropyl alcohol and a brush
No-clean flux
A small amount of safe residue
May be left on the board, **if the job allows it**; some standards and coatings still require cleaning
Water-soluble flux
Very active, and its residue is corrosive
**Must** be washed off soon after soldering, as the maker says, and the board dried

blocks.p: Add liquid or gel flux from a pen or syringe when you **rework an old joint, clear a bridge, use braid or solder surface-mount parts**: the flux in old solder was used up long ago. Use only electronics flux. Plumber's flux is acid and destroys boards.

ul: A tip is copper plated with iron. The plating is what makes it last. **Never file, sand or scrape a plated tip**: once the plating is broken, the solder eats the copper in days.

Keep the tip **tinned**: a thin bright coat of solder at all times. Wipe it on brass wool or a damp (not wet) sponge just before each joint, and put fresh solder on it before you put the iron back in the stand.
A tip that has gone black and will not take solder is cleaned with **tip tinner** (tip activator) or brass wool and then re-tinned. Turning the heat up makes it worse.
Turn the station down, or let it go into **sleep mode**, when it will not be used for a few minutes. A tip left hot and idle oxidises quickly and wears out early.
Replace tips that are pitted, holed or worn out of shape.
At the end of the session: tin the tip, switch off, leave the iron to cool in its stand, and clean the bench.

blocks.note: Good tip care is not housekeeping for its own sake. A clean, tinned tip passes heat into the joint in a second or two. A dirty tip passes almost none, so the trainee holds it on for longer and longer, and it is the board that suffers.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Making good joints: boards, wires and terminals

blocks.h: A through-hole joint, step by step

flow: Fix the board in a holder so both hands are free
Check the part, its value and its orientation; fit it flat to the board
Clean and tin the tip
Touch the tip to the pad and the lead together
After about a second, feed solder onto the joint, not onto the tip
Take the solder away, then the iron
Keep everything still until the solder sets
Trim the lead; inspect the joint

blocks.p: The whole joint should take about 2 to 4 seconds. Heat the **work** and let the work melt the solder: this is what makes the solder flow out and bond. That smooth flowing and bonding is called **wetting**.

blocks.h: What a good joint looks like

ul: A smooth, concave **fillet**: solder sloping up from the pad to the lead, like the foot of a volcano.
The outline of the lead still visible in the solder.
The pad fully covered, with solder feathering out to a thin edge.
On a **plated through-hole**, solder drawn through the hole, with a fillet on both sides of the board. The workmanship standard says how much fill is the minimum.
Tin-lead: bright and smooth. Lead-free: often duller and slightly grainy, which is normal.

blocks.note: Do not carry solder to the joint on the tip. By the time it arrives, its flux has burned away, so nothing cleans the joint, and you get a dull blob sitting on top of unwetted metal.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Orientation: parts that must go in the right way

head: Part
Marking
rows: Integrated circuit (IC)
A notch or dot marks pin 1 end; match it to the outline printed on the board
Electrolytic capacitor
A stripe marks the negative lead; the board is marked + or has a shaded half
Diode and LED
A band marks the cathode; an LED's shorter lead or flat side is the cathode
Connectors and ribbon cable
Pin 1 is marked on the connector and the board; on grey ribbon cable the red stripe is usually pin 1

blocks.p: Where an IC may need changing again, the design may use an **IC socket**: a holder soldered to the board that the IC plugs into. Fit sockets only where the maker's design allows; they are a poor choice where there is vibration.

blocks.h: Soldering wires to terminals and connector pins

flow: Slide heat-shrink sleeving onto the wire, well back from the joint
Strip the wire without nicking strands; twist and lightly tin the end
Hold the wire mechanically: wrap it part-way round the post, hook it through the tag, or seat it in the solder cup
Heat the terminal and the wire together and feed solder onto the joint
Keep it still until set; inspect
When cool, slide the heat-shrink over the joint and shrink it with a heat gun
Support the wire with a clamp, tie or boot so the joint carries no strain

ul: The wire is held **mechanically first** so that the solder only has to make the electrical connection. A wire just laid against a post and soldered relies on the solder for strength, and solder is weak.
Leave a small gap, about the wire's own diameter, between the end of the insulation and the solder. Insulation in the joint burns and contaminates it; a long bare gap can short to its neighbour.

Solder soaks a little way up the strands and makes that part of the wire **stiff**. Where the wire flexes or vibrates, it bends at the point where the stiff part ends, and breaks there. Keep the tinned length short and give the wire **strain relief**.
**Heat-shrink sleeving**, shrunk evenly with a heat gun, is the right insulation for a soldered joint. Tape unwinds in the heat; hot glue and bare joints are not insulation.

head: Situation
Why solder is wrong
Use instead
rows: A stranded conductor going into a screw or clamp terminal
Solder slowly flattens (creeps) under the pressure of the screw, so the terminal works loose and overheats
A crimped ferrule
Joints that will be shaken or flexed
The stiffened wire breaks where the solder ends
A crimped connector with strain relief
Large power conductors
The joint cannot be heated properly by hand, and solder softens if the joint runs hot
Crimped lugs or connectors made for the size
Hot places and fire-rated circuits
Solder can melt
The connection method the code and the specification require

blocks.p: Soldering is the normal method for parts on circuit boards and for small signal and control wires to connectors and terminal posts, where currents are small and the joint is supported.

A joint needs enough heat, quickly, in the right place. Too little gives a cold joint; too much, or too long, damages the board and the parts. Most heat problems are solved by getting heat **in faster**, not by turning the temperature up.

ul: **Large copper areas**: earth and power planes, wide tracks, the pads of relays, transformers and regulators.
**Thick, multilayer boards**: the copper layers inside draw heat away from the hole.
**Heavy leads and terminals**: screw-terminal blocks, connectors, heat sinks.

blocks.p: The amount of heat a tip can deliver depends on its **size (thermal mass)** and the **power** of the iron, as well as its temperature. A fine tip at 400 °C goes cold the moment it touches a large earth pad. A wide chisel tip at 350 °C, on a station with more power, makes the same joint in three seconds.

head: Problem
Poor fix
Better fix
rows: Solder will not flow on a large pad
Turn the station to maximum; hold the iron on for longer
A larger chisel tip or a more powerful iron; fresh flux; a clean, tinned tip
Thick multilayer board
A very hot tip held for a long time on each joint
Warm the whole board gently on a **board preheater** (often to about 100 °C) so that each joint needs less heat from the iron
A small, heat-sensitive part beside a heavy joint
Solder everything with one big, hot tip
A fine tip and short contact for the small part; clip a **heat sink** on its lead between the body and the joint
Heavy and delicate parts on the same board
Solder in any order
Solder the heavy joints first and the delicate parts last, so that they are not heated again

head: What you see
What happened
rows: Brown, dark or blistered board near the joint
The board material was overheated: too hot, for too long
A pad or track lifting from the board
The adhesive under the copper failed from heat, often with force on the lead as well
Black, crusty flux
The flux was burned; the tip was too hot or stayed too long
Melted plastic on a connector or switch; a discoloured part
The part's body was overheated
A dull, wrinkled joint that took many attempts
Repeated heating; flux exhausted

blocks.p: If a joint has not flowed within a few seconds, **stop**. Take the iron away, let the joint cool, and work out why: tip size, tip condition, flux, temperature. Then try again. Fifteen seconds of pressing harder is how pads are lifted.

A small **blowhole** or pinhole in a through-hole joint is usually made by gas or moisture escaping from the hole while the solder is still liquid. Boards that have been stored in damp air take up moisture. If blowholes keep appearing, the board may need drying before rework, by the method and at the temperature the maker gives.

blocks.note: Boards from equipment that has stood in a damp, salty place, such as a pump house, a gate motor box or a seaside villa, are often corroded and full of moisture. Clean and dry them before you judge the joints, and expect pads to lift more easily.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Tool
How it works
Good for
rows: De-soldering pump (solder sucker)
A spring-loaded plunger sucks up molten solder when released
Clearing through-holes and large joints; empty it often and keep its tip and seal clean
De-soldering braid (wick)
Fine copper braid soaks up molten solder when heated on the joint
Cleaning pads, clearing bridges, removing the last traces; works far better with added flux
Vacuum de-soldering station
A heated hollow tip and a vacuum pump clear a hole in one action
Multi-pin through-hole parts; keep the nozzle and filters clean
Hot tweezers
Two heated tips grip and melt both ends of a part at once
Small two-ended surface-mount parts
Hot-air rework station
Blows air at a set temperature and flow through a shaped nozzle
Surface-mount ICs and parts with several joints

flow: Board in a holder at the ESD bench; note or photograph the part's orientation
If the part is faulty and will be scrapped: cut each lead at the body, then remove the leads one at a time with the iron and tweezers
If the part must be saved: add flux and clear every hole with a pump or vacuum tool
Check that every pin is free, moving each one gently
Lift the part out without force
Clean the holes and pads with braid and flux
Inspect for lifted pads and damaged tracks before fitting the new part

blocks.p: **Never force a part out.** A pin still held by a film of solder will pull the plating out of the hole or the pad off the board. If a hole will not clear, add fresh solder and flux and try again: new solder helps old solder to melt and flow.

To fit the new part: check its orientation, solder two opposite corner pins, check that it sits flat and the right way round, then solder the rest, moving about the part so that heat does not build up in one place.
**Surface-mount technology (SMT)** parts sit on pads on the surface of the board, with no holes. They are small, so use fine solder wire, added flux, tweezers, good light and magnification.

head: Task
Method
rows: Fit a two-ended part (chip resistor or capacitor)
Put a little solder on **one** pad. Hold the part with tweezers, reheat that pad and slide the part into place so it sits flat. Solder the other end. Then reflow the first end with a touch of flux.
Remove a two-ended part
Hot tweezers on both ends at once, or hot air; lift as soon as both ends melt. Heating one end at a time tears the pads.
Fit a multi-pin IC
Flux the pads, align the IC and tack two opposite corners. Solder each pin, or drag a fluxed bevel tip along the row.
Clear bridges between fine-pitch pins
Add flux, lay braid across the bridged pins and heat it so that it draws off the extra solder; or drag a clean, fluxed tip along the pins. Never cut between pins with a knife.
Remove an IC with hot air
Choose the nozzle for the part, set the temperature and air flow as the maker says, heat evenly and lift with tweezers when all joints have melted.

blocks.h: Using hot air without collateral damage

ul: Hot air heats everything it reaches. **Shield nearby parts** with heat-resistant tape or small metal shields, so they are not overheated, loosened or blown off their pads.
Use a nozzle no bigger than needed, and the **lowest air flow** that does the job: a strong flow blows small parts away.
Keep the nozzle moving in small circles above the part.
A small part that stands up on one end after soldering (a 'tombstone') was heated or wetted unevenly: one end melted and pulled before the other. Reflow it with flux, holding it flat.

blocks.p: If a pad lifts or a track breaks, do not hide it under a blob of solder or glue. **Record it**, tell your supervisor, and repair it by a method the customer or the workmanship standard approves. The usual repair for a broken or lifted track is a **jumper wire**: a short insulated wire soldered between the two sound points the track used to join, routed neatly and fixed down. Some customers do not accept repaired boards at all; that is their decision, not yours.

At work, joints are judged against a **written workmanship standard**: the customer's or the company's own, often based on an industry standard such as IPC-A-610. A written standard means that every inspector gives the same answer, whoever did the work. Inspect under good light with a magnifier or bench microscope, and look at **both sides** of the board.

head: Defect
What it looks like
Usual cause
Correction
rows: Cold joint
Dull, lumpy solder balled up on the lead or pad, not wetted
Too little heat; dirty tip or surfaces; solder carried on the tip
Add flux and reflow with proper heat
Disturbed joint
Rough, frosty surface, often with a crack round the lead
The lead or board moved while the solder was setting
Add flux and reflow; hold everything still
Too little solder
A thin fillet; pad not covered; hole only part-filled
Solder taken away too soon
Add flux and solder, and reheat until the hole fills
Too much solder
A ball that hides the lead's outline; may reach the next pad
Too much wire fed in
Remove the excess with braid, then reflow
Bridge
Solder joining two pads or pins that should be separate
Too much solder; pins close together
Flux and braid
Spike (icicle)
A sharp point of solder standing up from the joint
Iron taken away slowly; flux used up; tip not hot enough
Add flux and reflow briefly
Solder balls and splashes
Tiny beads of solder on the board, often stuck in flux
Too much solder or flux; spitting; flicking
Remove them all: a loose ball can short two pins later
Blowhole
A small pit or hole in the fillet
Gas or moisture escaping from the hole
Reflow; dry the board if it keeps happening
Lifted pad, burnt board
Copper raised from the board; brown or blistered board
Too much heat, time or force
Record it; approved repair only

blocks.p: Also check: the right parts, in the right places, the right way round and seated flat; leads trimmed to length; no damaged insulation; flux cleaned where required; nothing left on the board.

blocks.note: Do not reject a lead-free joint just because it is dull or grainy. Judge it by its shape and wetting: a smooth concave fillet that has flowed onto the pad and the lead.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Visual inspection under magnification
With no power: check for short circuits across the supply rails with a multimeter
With no power: check the parts you changed (continuity, resistance, diode test)
Power from a current-limited bench supply at the rated voltage, with a low limit
Watch the current: normal, or straight to the limit?
Check the board's supply voltages at the test points
Check the function of the repaired section
Refit in the equipment with the supply isolated, then do a final function test
Record the tests and the results

blocks.p: A **current-limited bench supply** lets you set the most current the board can take. If there is a short or a reversed part, the supply holds the current at the limit and its voltage drops, instead of feeding in enough energy to burn tracks. If that happens, **switch off and find the fault**; do not raise the limit to 'push through'. Never use a higher voltage than the board's rating, and never test a low-voltage board from a car battery or straight from the mains: both can deliver a very large current into a fault.

A wiring harness is tested for **continuity** of every wire, end to end, against the wiring list, and for **shorts** between every wire and its neighbours (the meter should show an open circuit), before any supply is connected.

head: Record
Example
rows: Board or equipment identity
Pump controller, serial 04417, from panel P2
Fault found
No output to relay K1; U3 pin 7 short to earth
Work done and parts changed
U3 replaced; R12 replaced; lead-free solder
Damage and repairs
Pad lifted at U3 pin 9; jumper fitted, approved by supervisor
Inspection and test results
Passed visual; no shorts; 12.1 V at TP2; relay operates
Who did the work, who inspected it, and the date
Names and date

blocks.p: Mark the board as passed or rejected. A record that says only 'fixed' helps nobody when the board comes back.

head: What you see
What to say and show
rows: Solder carried to the joint on the tip
The flux has burned off before it reaches the joint. Heat the joint, then feed the wire onto it.
The iron held on a joint for 10 or 15 seconds
Stop. Check the tip size, clean and tin it, add flux, then try again.
The station turned to maximum 'to make it flow'
Heat that high burns flux and lifts pads. Use a bigger tip or preheat.
A black tip being filed
Filing removes the plating. Use tip tinner and re-tin.
Solder flicked off the tip
It can hit someone's eye. Wipe the tip on the cleaner.
Parts handled with no strap, or a strap not tested
The damage cannot be seen. Test the strap, record it, then carry on.
An IC being levered out while some pins are still held
Stop before the pads come off. Clear every pin first, or cut the leads if the part is scrap.

blocks.p: Have each trainee inspect another's work against the written criteria: people learn to see defects in someone else's joints before they see them in their own.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can find out a board's solder type and the maker's rework rules before starting.
I can isolate equipment, prove it dead and check capacitors for stored charge before removing a board.
I can control fumes, lead, burns, splashes, fire and waste at the bench.
I can set up an ESD-protected bench, test a wrist strap and handle sensitive parts.
I can choose a tip, a temperature, a solder and a flux for a joint, and explain my choice.
I can explain the differences between 63/37, 60/40 and lead-free solder, and why they are not mixed.
I can look after tips and check the real tip temperature.
I can make and recognise a good through-hole joint and a good wire-to-terminal joint.
I can say when a crimped or screwed connection is better than a soldered one, and why.
I can plan the soldering of a board with heavy copper and heat-sensitive parts.
I can remove and replace a multi-pin through-hole part without damaging the board.
I can fit and remove two-ended surface-mount parts and clear bridges on a fine-pitch IC.
I can use hot air without damaging nearby parts.
I can deal correctly with a lifted pad or broken track.
I can inspect work against a written standard and name the common defects, their causes and their corrections.
I can test a repaired board in the right order, using a current-limited supply.
I can complete a rework record.
I can set bench rules and correct poor technique in others.

terms: Blowhole
A small pit in a joint made by gas or moisture escaping while the solder was liquid.
Braid (wick)
Fine copper braid that soaks up molten solder.
Bridge
Unwanted solder joining two pads or pins.
Cold joint
A joint that did not get enough heat to wet: dull, lumpy and unreliable.
Current-limited supply
A bench supply that holds the current at a set maximum.
De-soldering pump
A spring-loaded tool that sucks up molten solder; also called a solder sucker.
Dross
Oxide and waste skimmed from the surface of molten solder.
EPA
ESD-protected area: a marked area where static is controlled.
ESD
Electrostatic discharge: the sudden flow of static charge.
Eutectic
An alloy that changes straight from liquid to solid at one temperature, such as 63/37 tin-lead.
Fillet
The smooth, concave slope of solder between a lead and its pad.
Flux
A material that removes oxide and helps solder to wet the metal.
Heat sink (clip-on)
A metal clip put on a lead to draw heat away from a sensitive part.
IC socket
A holder soldered to the board so that an IC can be plugged in and changed.
Jumper wire
A short wire soldered in to replace a broken or lifted track.
No-clean flux
Flux whose small residue may be left on the board if the job allows.
Preheater
A heater that warms the whole board before and during rework.
Rework station
A bench machine that blows controlled hot air to remove and refit surface-mount parts.
SAC
Tin-silver-copper: the most common family of lead-free solders.
SMT
Surface-mount technology: parts soldered to pads on the board's surface.
Tinning
Coating a tip or a wire with a thin layer of solder.
Tip thermometer
An instrument with a sensor pad that measures the real temperature of a tip.
Wetting
Solder flowing out smoothly and bonding to clean metal.

c1.title: A pump controller from Mile Gully
c1.text: Technician Mr Lascelles Brown and Level 3 trainee Sherika Daley must repair the control board from a 220 V borehole-pump panel at a community water scheme near Mile Gully, Manchester. The panel has been isolated, locked off and proved dead. The board has a large mains filter capacitor, a failed 14-pin through-hole IC, and wide copper areas round the pads of the pump relay. The service sheet says the board was made with lead-free solder. The repair bench also has a reel of 63/37 tin-lead solder.

c2.title: An ESD bench in Spanish Town
c2.text: Kamar Wright, a Level 3 trainee, is setting up a bench for repairing CCTV recorder boards at a repair shop in Spanish Town, St Catherine. The room is air-conditioned and the air is dry. On the bench are a dissipative mat whose earth lead is hanging loose, two wrist straps, a strap tester and a new memory chip in a silvery shielding bag. When Kamar tests his wrist strap, the tester shows 'fail'.

c3.title: LED driver boards in Montego Bay
c3.text: At a sign shop in Montego Bay, St James, trainee Ricardo Haughton is reworking lead-free LED driver boards. Each has tiny chip resistors packed close together and a fine-pitch IC. He replaces two chip resistors with a hot-air tool, and clears solder bridges on the IC with flux and braid. While he heats the first resistor, a neighbouring one is blown off its pads. Afterwards, one of the new resistors is standing up on one end.

c4.title: A control harness for a Bog Walk juice plant
c4.text: At a juice plant in Bog Walk, St Catherine, Level 3 trainee Tashana Morgan is making a 24 V control harness for a filling machine that vibrates as it runs. The drawing calls for wires soldered into the solder cups of a multi-pin connector, with heat-shrink sleeving over every soldered joint and a cable clamp on the connector. On her first few wires, solder has soaked about 10 mm up the strands under the insulation.

c5.title: A repair bench in Harbour View
c5.text: Mrs Paulette Jarrett runs the repair bench of a security company in Harbour View, St Andrew, and checks trainees' rework against the company's written workmanship standard. On trainee Odane's 12 V alarm board she finds a joint with a rough, frosty surface and a fine crack round the lead; a sharp spike of solder standing up from another joint; and several tiny solder balls stuck in flux beside an IC. When the board is powered from the bench supply with the current limit set to 100 mA, the current goes straight to the limit and the voltage drops to 2 V.

questions.q: The panel has been proved dead. What should Sherika check next, before she handles the board?
o: That the pump motor has stopped turning and is cool to the touch
That the board's solder mask is not scratched anywhere near the IC
That the filter capacitor's voltage has fallen to a safe level
That the station's tip is hot enough for lead-free solder work
questions.why: A mains filter capacitor can hold a dangerous charge long after the supply is off. Measure across it with a suitable meter; if it is still charged, discharge it through a suitable resistor or tool as the maker says, and measure again.

questions.q: Which solder should be used to fit the new IC?
o: Lead-free solder, as the board was made with it
63/37 tin-lead, because it flows more easily
63/37 tin-lead on the top side, lead-free below
Whichever reel is nearer, as both will conduct
questions.why: Rework uses the alloy the board was made with. Mixing tin-lead into a lead-free joint can form a weaker joint that cracks in service, and it breaks the maker's rules for the board. Keep separate tips and braid for each alloy.

questions.q: Solder will not flow on the relay pads, so Sherika turns the station to its maximum, 450 °C. What is the likely result?
o: A stronger joint, because hotter solder bonds better
A brighter joint, as lead-free solder shines at 450 °C
No change, as the tip cannot heat a board past 220 °C
Burnt flux and lifted pads, and still a poor joint
questions.why: The wide copper carries heat away faster than a small tip can supply it, whatever its temperature. Extra degrees burn the flux and weaken the bond under the pads. A larger chisel tip, a more powerful iron or preheating gets heat in faster.

questions.q: How should Sherika make sure the new IC goes in the right way round?
o: Fit it so its printed type number reads from the board's top edge
Match its notch or dot to the outline on the board and her photo
Fit it either way, since a 14-pin IC is the same from both ends
Match it to the way the nearest capacitor has been fitted
questions.why: The notch or dot marks the pin 1 end, and the board's printed outline shows where it goes. A photo or note taken before removal is a second check. An IC fitted backwards is usually destroyed at power-up, and may take other parts with it.

questions.q: What does the dissipative mat do while its earth lead hangs loose?
o: It still drains charge, but more slowly than it normally would
It cannot drain charge away, so it gives no protection
It protects the parts on the bench, but not the person working
It builds up heat under the soldering station and its stand
questions.why: The mat works by giving charge a controlled path to earth. With no connection there is no path, so charge stays on the mat and on anything placed on it. The lead goes to the bench's common earth point, with the wrist strap.

questions.q: Kamar's wrist strap fails on the tester. What should he do?
o: Carry on, but touch the bench frame every few minutes
Carry on, as the mat will protect the boards by itself
Tighten the band and start work without testing again
Handle no parts until a strap passes the test
questions.why: A failed test means there is no reliable path from his body to earth: a broken lead, a worn band or a poor fit. He fixes or replaces the strap, tests again, records the pass and only then handles sensitive parts.

questions.q: Why does the shop's dry, air-conditioned air make ESD control more important?
o: Dry air makes solder set too quickly
Dry air lets static charge build up more easily
Dry air stops the wrist strap's resistor working
Dry air makes flux fumes harder to extract
questions.why: In humid air, a thin film of moisture on surfaces lets charge leak away. In dry air, charge stays where it forms, so walking, clothing and packaging build up much higher voltages. The straps and mat matter most in dry rooms.

questions.q: When should the new memory chip be taken out of its shielding bag?
o: At the ESD bench, with a tested strap on, just before fitting
At the stores counter, so the part number can be checked and signed for
As soon as it arrives, so that it can reach room temperature in time
The day before, so that it is laid out ready on the bench for the job
questions.why: The bag shields the chip from static until it is inside the protected area. Opened anywhere else, or left lying out, the chip is exposed to charge from hands, clothing and packaging, and the damage cannot be seen.

questions.q: Which change would best stop the hot-air tool blowing neighbouring parts off the board?
o: A higher temperature, so the job is over sooner
A wider nozzle held further away from the board
A lower air flow, a smaller nozzle and shielding
A stronger air flow aimed straight down at the part
questions.why: Hot air melts the joints of everything it reaches, and a strong flow then pushes loose parts off their pads. The lowest flow that does the job, a nozzle sized to the part and heat-resistant tape or shields over the neighbours keep the heat where it is wanted.

questions.q: One new chip resistor is standing up on one end. What most likely caused it?
o: Static damage to the resistor before it was fitted
The wrong value of resistor for that position
Lead-free solder, which always lifts small parts
One end melted and pulled before the other
questions.why: If one pad's solder melts first, its surface tension pulls that end down and tips the part up: a 'tombstone'. Even heating, the right amount of solder on each pad and holding the part flat while reflowing with flux prevent it.

questions.q: After the bridges are cleared, the IC's joints look duller and grainier than the tin-lead joints Ricardo is used to. What should he conclude?
o: They are cold joints and must all be reflowed
That is normal; judge them by shape and wetting
The flux was the wrong type for this board
The braid has taken too much solder off each pin
questions.why: Lead-free solder sets with a duller, slightly grainy surface even when the joint is good. What matters is a smooth fillet that has wetted both the pin and the pad. Reflowing sound joints only adds heat and risk.

questions.q: Why must Ricardo inspect the fine-pitch IC under magnification after clearing the bridges?
o: Magnification shows whether the IC is static damaged
Company rules require a photograph of every board
Hair-thin bridges and cracks cannot be seen by eye
The lens shows the temperature each joint reached
questions.why: Pins on a fine-pitch IC are a fraction of a millimetre apart. A thread of solder between two of them, or a joint that has not wetted its pad, is invisible without a magnifier or microscope but will stop the board working.

questions.q: Why must Tashana slide the heat-shrink sleeving onto each wire before she solders it into the connector?
o: It cannot be put on once the wire is soldered
It holds the strands together while they are tinned
It stops solder from flowing into the solder cup
It keeps the wire cool while the joint is made
questions.why: Once the wire is fixed in the connector, there is no free end to slide a sleeve over. It goes on first and is kept well back, so the heat of soldering does not shrink it early. It is slid over the joint and shrunk when the joint has cooled.

questions.q: On this machine, why is the solder that has soaked 10 mm up the strands a problem?
o: The wire will carry less current than its rating allows
The stiff length can crack where it meets flexible wire
The solder will melt again when the machine warms up fully
The heat-shrink will not grip a tinned wire when shrunk
questions.why: Solder turns flexible stranded wire into a stiff rod. Under vibration the wire bends at the point where the stiff part ends, and breaks there. Keep the tinned length short, and clamp the cable so that the joints carry no movement.

questions.q: How much bare wire should be left between the end of the insulation and the solder cup?
o: None: the insulation should sit inside the cup
About 10 mm, to keep the insulation cool
About the length of the solder cup itself
A small gap, about the wire's own diameter
questions.why: Insulation inside the joint burns and contaminates the solder. A long bare gap can touch the next pin. A gap of about one wire diameter keeps the insulation out of the heat and is covered by the heat-shrink.

questions.q: Before the harness is powered, which test shows that the wire on pin 7 is not touching the wire on pin 8?
o: A voltage reading on pin 7 with the supply switched on
A continuity test from end to end of pin 7's wire alone
A resistance reading between the two wires, unpowered
A pull test on each of the two soldered joints in turn
questions.why: With the harness unpowered, the meter between two separate wires should show an open circuit. An end-to-end continuity test proves that a wire is connected, not that it is clear of its neighbour, so both tests are done on every wire.

questions.q: What most likely caused the joint with the frosty surface and the crack round the lead?
o: The lead moved while the solder was setting
Too much solder was fed into the joint
The board was cleaned with the wrong solvent
The wrist strap was not connected
questions.why: This is a disturbed joint: movement as the solder passed from liquid to solid left a rough surface and a crack. It may conduct today and fail later. It is reflowed with fresh flux, with the board and lead held still.

questions.q: The board may work with the solder balls left where they are. Why must they still be removed?
o: They make the board heavier than its drawing allows
They show that the wrong alloy of solder was used
A ball can come loose later and short two pins
They slowly draw solder away from the good joints
questions.why: A solder ball held only by flux can be freed by vibration, heat or cleaning, and then roll between two pins or tracks. The defect is cleared before the board leaves, and too much solder, spitting flux or flicking is looked for as the cause.

questions.q: At power-up the current goes straight to the 100 mA limit and the voltage falls to 2 V. What should be done?
o: Raise the limit to 2 A so the board can start up
Switch off and look for a short or reversed part
Leave it on for a few minutes to see if it settles
Connect it to the alarm panel's own supply instead
questions.why: The supply is holding the current at its limit because the board is drawing far more than it should: a bridge, a short or a part fitted backwards. The limit has protected the board. Raising it, or using a supply with no limit, would burn tracks or parts.

questions.q: What caused the sharp spike of solder on Odane's joint, and how is it put right?
o: Static discharge; replace the part and solder it again
Too large a tip; change to a fine conical tip and leave it
Moisture in the board; bake the board and leave the joint
Flux used up as the iron left; add flux and reflow briefly
questions.why: A spike forms when solder is dragged out as the iron leaves a joint whose flux is spent or which is not quite hot enough. Fresh flux and a brief reflow let surface tension pull the solder back into a smooth fillet. A spike can pierce insulation or short to a neighbour.
